modules.title: Course Overview & Science Update
modules.subtitle: What's New in PALS 2025
learningObjectives: Describe the purpose and components of the PALS course.
Identify key BLS and ALS science updates in the 2025 guidelines.
Understand the links in the Chain of Survival.

points.heading: Target Audience & Purpose
points.body: PALS is designed for healthcare professionals (HCPs) who manage respiratory and cardiovascular emergencies in pediatric patients. The primary goal is to improve outcomes by preparing HCPs to effectively recognize and intervene in respiratory emergencies, shock, and cardiac arrest.

points.heading: Foundation of PALS
points.body: Without high-quality BLS, PALS interventions will fail. Basic Life Support is the cornerstone of successful resuscitation.

quiz.stem: Who is the PALS course specifically designed for?
quiz.rationale: PALS is specifically designed for HCPs who manage respiratory and cardiovascular emergencies in pediatric patients.

quiz.stem: What is the passing threshold for the PALS written exam?
quiz.rationale: The written exam requires a score of 84% to pass.

points.heading: Course Components
points.body: The PALS Provider Course includes: BLS competency testing, skills stations (Airway, Vascular Access, Rhythm/Electrical Therapy), case scenario discussions, simulations, and a written exam requiring 84% to pass.

points.heading: Precourse Preparation
points.body: Students are required to complete precourse preparation, including self-assessment modules and reviewing the provider manual, to ensure a baseline understanding of ECG rhythms and pharmacology.

points.heading: Historical Context
points.body: PALS was first developed by the AHA in the 1980s and has been updated multiple times to reflect evolving evidence in pediatric resuscitation science.

points.heading: International Adaptations
points.body: The core PALS curriculum is adapted internationally by various resuscitation councils to align with local healthcare systems and resources.

points.heading: Critical Recognition
points.body: Immediate recognition of cardiac arrest remains critical for improving outcomes.

points.heading: Infant Compressions Technique Change
points.body: The 2-finger technique has been ELIMINATED for infant compressions. Rescuers should use the heel-of-1-hand or 2-thumb encircling hands technique.

points.heading: Advanced Airway Ventilation Rate
points.body: The respiratory rate for pediatric patients with an advanced airway in place is 20-30 breaths/min.

points.heading: Compressions and Ventilations
points.body: Providing both ventilation and compressions improves Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest (OHCA) survival in pediatric patients.

points.heading: FBAO Updates
points.body: For Foreign-Body Airway Obstruction (FBAO), back blows combined with abdominal thrusts are now recommended for BOTH infants and children.

points.heading: Opioid Overdose
points.body: Administer naloxone for suspected opioid overdose, but do not delay standard CPR.

quiz.stem: Which chest compression technique was eliminated for infants in the 2025 guidelines?
quiz.rationale: The 2-finger technique was eliminated due to evidence showing it was less effective at achieving proper depth.

quiz.stem: What is the new recommended respiratory rate for a pediatric patient with an advanced airway?
quiz.rationale: The recommended rate is 20-30 breaths/min.

points.heading: Evidence for Elimination of 2-Finger Technique
points.body: Studies have shown that the 2-finger technique often fails to achieve the adequate compression depth required for high-quality CPR in infants, leading to its removal from the guidelines.

points.heading: Importance of Ventilation
points.body: Because pediatric cardiac arrests are predominantly asphyxial (respiratory origin) rather than primary cardiac events, ventilation is crucial to restore oxygenation and improve survival odds.

points.heading: ILCOR CoSTR Process
points.body: Guidelines are developed based on the International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation (ILCOR) Consensus on Science with Treatment Recommendations (CoSTR), which continuously evaluates resuscitation science.

points.heading: Epinephrine Administration
points.body: Early administration of epinephrine is prioritized for nonshockable rhythms to improve outcomes.

points.heading: Defibrillation
points.body: Rapid defibrillation remains the absolute priority for shockable rhythms.

points.heading: Diastolic BP Targets During CPR
points.body: Target diastolic blood pressure during CPR is ≥25 mmHg in infants and ≥30 mmHg in children.

points.heading: ETCO2 Monitoring
points.body: End-Tidal CO2 (ETCO2) is recommended as an indicator of CPR quality, but it should not be used in isolation to decide when to terminate resuscitation efforts.

points.heading: Post-Arrest Care
points.body: Actively prevent hyperthermia (>37.5°C) post-arrest. Post-arrest blood pressure thresholds aim for >10th percentile for age and sex.

points.heading: Neuroprognostication
points.body: Multimodal neuroprognostication is required; no single test is sufficient to predict neurological outcomes.

quiz.stem: What is the target diastolic blood pressure during CPR for an infant?
quiz.rationale: The 2025 target is ≥25 mmHg for infants.

quiz.stem: Which temperature must be actively avoided post-cardiac arrest?
quiz.rationale: Hyperthermia (>37.5°C) must be prevented post-arrest to protect neurological function.

points.heading: 2020 vs 2025 Differences
points.body: The 2025 guidelines provide more specific hemodynamic targets during CPR and stricter parameters for multimodal neuroprognostication compared to 2020.

points.heading: Blood Pressure Tables
points.body: The 2025 guidelines include updated, simplified blood pressure tables to help providers quickly identify the 10th percentile thresholds by age.

points.heading: Post-Discharge Challenges
points.body: Cardiac arrest survivors often face significant long-term physical, cognitive, and emotional challenges, highlighting the need for comprehensive rehabilitation plans post-discharge.

points.heading: The 6 Links
points.body:
1. Recognition & prevention
2. High-quality CPR
3. Defibrillation
4. ALS interventions
5. Post-cardiac arrest care
6. Recovery

points.heading: Interdependence
points.body: Each link in the chain is independent yet completely connected. A broken link leads to decreased survival outcomes.

quiz.stem: What is the final link in the Chain of Survival?
quiz.rationale: Recovery is the 6th and final link.

quiz.stem: How many total links are in the pediatric Chain of Survival?
quiz.rationale: There are 6 links in the chain.

points.heading: Unified Chain
points.body: The 2025 unified chain applies across infants, children, and adults, emphasizing consistent principles across all age groups.

points.heading: Newborn Chain
points.body: A separate Newborn Chain of Care exists specifically for resuscitation at birth, which focuses heavily on establishing adequate ventilation.

points.heading: Evolution of the Chain
points.body: The Chain of Survival concept was introduced by the AHA to visually emphasize the critical, sequential actions needed to treat sudden cardiac arrest. 'Recovery' was added as the 6th link in recent years to highlight survivorship.

modules.title: BLS & AED Review
modules.subtitle: Master High-Quality CPR
learningObjectives: Define pediatric age categories for BLS.
Perform single and multi-rescuer BLS sequences.
Demonstrate proper chest compression and ventilation techniques.
Manage foreign-body airway obstructions and opioid emergencies.

points.heading: Infant vs. Child
points.body: Infant = <1 year of age (excluding newborns in the delivery room). Child = 1 year to the onset of puberty.

points.heading: Signs of Puberty
points.body: Chest or underarm hair in males; breast development in females.

points.heading: BLS vs. ALS Scope
points.body: BLS pediatric guidance applies to infants and prepubertal children. ALS pediatric guidance applies to patients up to 18 years of age.

quiz.stem: For the purposes of BLS, what defines a 'child'?
options: 1 year of age up to 18 years
1 year of age up to puberty
1 month of age up to puberty
1 year of age up to 12 years
quiz.rationale: A child is defined as 1 year to puberty for BLS guidelines.

points.heading: Why Definitions Differ
points.body: BLS guidelines distinguish prepubertal children because body size determines the appropriate compression technique. ALS covers up to 18 years as physiological and pharmacological responses remain 'pediatric' until adulthood.

points.heading: Neonatal Resuscitation Program (NRP)
points.body: The neonatal period (especially in the delivery room) is governed by NRP guidelines, which differ significantly from infant BLS.

points.heading: The Sequence
points.body:
1. Ensure scene safety.
2. Check responsiveness and shout for help.
3. Assess breathing and pulse simultaneously (max 10 seconds).

points.heading: Pulse Check Locations
points.body: Infant: Brachial pulse. Child: Carotid or Femoral pulse.

points.heading: No Pulse Identified
points.body: Begin 30:2 ratio of compressions to breaths.

points.heading: When to Activate EMS
points.body: Witnessed collapse: Activate EMS and get AED immediately. Unwitnessed collapse: Perform 2 minutes of CPR first, then activate EMS/get AED.

quiz.stem: What is the compression-to-ventilation ratio for a single rescuer performing CPR on an infant?
quiz.rationale: Single rescuers always use a 30:2 ratio.

quiz.stem: Where should you check the pulse on an unresponsive 6-month-old?
quiz.rationale: The brachial artery is preferred in infants.

points.heading: Why Brachial for Infants?
points.body: Infants have short, chubby necks, making the carotid artery difficult to locate reliably. The brachial pulse is much more accessible.

points.heading: Agonal Gasps
points.body: Agonal breathing can mimic normal breathing but is a sign of cardiac arrest. It is not normal breathing.

points.heading: Pulse Landmarks
points.body: Brachial: inside upper arm between elbow and shoulder. Carotid: side of the neck. Femoral: inner thigh at the crease.

points.heading: Ratios by Age
points.body: Prepuberty: 15:2 with 2 rescuers. Puberty and older: 30:2 with 2 rescuers.

points.heading: Roles & Switching
points.body: One rescuer performs compressions, the other manages the airway and ventilation. Switch roles every 2 minutes (or 10 cycles of 15:2) to prevent fatigue.

quiz.stem: What is the multi-rescuer CPR ratio for a 5-year-old child?
quiz.rationale: For prepubertal children, the 2-rescuer ratio is 15:2.

points.heading: Why 15:2 for Pediatrics?
points.body: Pediatric cardiac arrests are most commonly respiratory in origin. The 15:2 ratio provides more frequent ventilations to address severe hypoxia.

points.heading: Compression-Only CPR
points.body: While compression-only CPR is heavily promoted for adults, it has severe limitations in pediatric populations due to the high incidence of asphyxial arrest.

points.heading: Infant Technique
points.body: Use the heel-of-1-hand OR the 2-thumb encircling hands technique (if the chest can be encircled). Compress the lower half of the sternum.

points.heading: Infant Depth & Rate
points.body: Depth: ≥1/3 AP diameter (~4 cm or 1.5 inches). Rate: 100-120/min. Allow full chest recoil.

points.heading: Child Technique
points.body: Use 1 or 2 hands on the center of the chest (lower half of sternum). Depth: ≥1/3 AP diameter (~5 cm or 2 inches). Rate: 100-120/min.

points.heading: Eliminated Technique
points.body: The 2-finger technique for infant compressions has been ELIMINATED.

quiz.stem: What is the correct chest compression depth for an infant?
quiz.rationale: Infant depth should be approximately 4 cm (1.5 inches) or ≥1/3 the AP diameter.

quiz.stem: What is the target compression rate?
quiz.rationale: The rate is 100 to 120 compressions per minute.

points.heading: Choosing the Infant Technique
points.body: The 2-thumb encircling technique is preferred if the rescuer's hands can comfortably encircle the infant's chest, as it generally produces better depth and coronary perfusion pressure.

points.heading: Rescuer Fatigue
points.body: Quality degrades significantly after just 1-2 minutes of compressions. Feedback devices (auditory or visual) are highly encouraged to maintain rate and depth.

points.heading: Rescue Breathing Rates
points.body: If a pulse is present but breathing is absent/abnormal: deliver 1 breath every 2-3 seconds (20-30 breaths/min). Recheck the pulse every 2 minutes.

points.heading: When to Start CPR Despite a Pulse
points.body: Start CPR if the heart rate is <60/min WITH signs of poor perfusion.

points.heading: Signs of Poor Perfusion
points.body: Cool extremities, weak pulses, pallor/mottling/cyanosis, and declining consciousness.

quiz.stem: What is the rescue breathing rate for a child with a pulse?
quiz.rationale: The rate is 1 breath every 2-3 seconds (20-30 breaths/min).

quiz.stem: A 2-year-old has a heart rate of 50/min and exhibits pallor and weak pulses. What is your next action?
quiz.rationale: Start CPR because the HR is <60/min with signs of poor perfusion.

points.heading: Airway Opening Techniques
points.body: Use the head-tilt chin-lift for most patients. Use the jaw thrust maneuver if a cervical spine injury is suspected.

points.heading: Adequate Ventilation
points.body: The primary measure of adequate ventilation is visible chest rise. Avoid excessive volume to prevent gastric inflation.

points.heading: Pad Selection
points.body: Use pediatric pads/dose attenuators if the patient is <8 years old. If pediatric pads are unavailable, standard adult pads MUST be used.

points.heading: Pad Placement
points.body: Ensure pads do not touch or overlap. Follow AED voice prompts. Resume CPR immediately after shock delivery.

quiz.stem: You are treating a 4-year-old in cardiac arrest and the AED only has adult pads. What should you do?
options: Wait for EMS to bring pediatric pads
Cut the adult pads in half
Use the adult pads, ensuring they do not overlap
Do not use the AED on this patient
quiz.rationale: Use the adult pads (often placing one on the front and one on the back to avoid overlap) because a shock is necessary to save the patient's life.

points.heading: Anterior-Posterior Placement
points.body: If the pads are too large for the child's chest and risk overlapping, place one pad on the center of the chest and the other on the center of the back.

points.heading: Energy Doses
points.body: Pediatric pads typically reduce the energy dose to approximately 50 Joules, appropriate for a child under 8 years or <25 kg.

points.heading: The 2025 Change
points.body: Back blows and abdominal thrusts are now recommended for BOTH infants AND children. (Previously, only back blows/chest thrusts were used for infants).

points.heading: The Cycle
points.body: Deliver cycles of 5 back blows alternating with 5 abdominal thrusts for a responsive choking patient.

points.heading: Unresponsive Patient
points.body: If the patient becomes unresponsive, lower them to the ground, begin CPR (do not check pulse first), and look into the mouth for the object before delivering breaths.

quiz.stem: What is the new 2025 FBAO recommendation for a conscious choking 4-year-old?
options: Alternating 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts
quiz.rationale: The 2025 update recommends alternating 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts for both infants and children.

points.heading: Positioning
points.body: For infants, lay them face down along your forearm, supporting the head/jaw, to deliver back blows. For abdominal thrusts, stand behind the child.

points.heading: Epidemiology
points.body: Choking is a leading cause of accidental death in young children, with food items and small toys being the most common culprits.

points.heading: Naloxone Administration
points.body: If a patient exhibits signs of an opioid overdose (respiratory depression or arrest), administer naloxone if available.

points.heading: Do Not Delay CPR
points.body: Never delay the start of standard CPR (compressions and ventilations) to retrieve or administer naloxone.

quiz.stem: Should CPR be delayed to administer naloxone in a suspected opioid overdose?
options: Yes, naloxone reverses the primary issue.
No, CPR takes priority and should not be delayed.
Yes, but only if the naloxone is readily available in the room.
No, naloxone is contraindicated in pediatric cardiac arrest.
quiz.rationale: Do not delay CPR; providing oxygen via ventilations and maintaining circulation is the critical priority.

points.heading: Routes and Dosing
points.body: Naloxone can be given via intramuscular (IM), intranasal (IN), or intravenous (IV) routes. The typical pediatric dose is 0.1 mg/kg.

points.heading: The Opioid Crisis
points.body: Opioid ingestions in the pediatric population (often accidental from household exposures) have steadily increased, making naloxone training essential for all HCPs.

modules.title: High-Performance Teams
modules.subtitle: Effective Communication and Dynamics
learningObjectives: Identify the 6 roles of a resuscitation team.
Practice closed-loop communication.
Demonstrate constructive team dynamics.

points.heading: The 6 Roles
points.body:
1. Team Leader
2. Compressor
3. Airway/Ventilation
4. IV/IO/Medications
5. Monitor/Defibrillator
6. Recorder/Timer

points.heading: Team Leader Function
points.body: The Team Leader assigns roles, monitors performance, and maintains global situational awareness.

quiz.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the 6 standard resuscitation team roles?
quiz.rationale: While a family liaison is useful, it is not one of the 6 core clinical resuscitation roles.

points.heading: Role Doubling
points.body: In smaller teams, roles must be combined. For instance, the Airway person might also manage the Monitor/Defibrillator, or the Team Leader might handle Medications.

points.heading: Crew Resource Management (CRM)
points.body: These team dynamics are derived from aviation CRM principles, adapted to reduce human error in high-stress medical environments.

points.heading: Closed-Loop Communication
points.body:
1. Team Leader gives order.
2. Team member repeats back the order.
3. Team Leader confirms the message was heard correctly.

points.heading: Key Elements
points.body: Clear messages, mutual respect, and constructive intervention if a team member observes a potential error.

quiz.stem: What is the primary purpose of closed-loop communication?
options: To document actions for legal purposes
To ensure commands are heard and understood exactly as intended
To maintain quiet in the trauma bay
To allow the recorder to keep track of time
quiz.rationale: Closed-loop communication ensures shared mental models and prevents medication/action errors.

points.heading: SBAR Technique
points.body: SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) is heavily utilized during handoffs to summarize the patient's status effectively.

points.heading: Communication Impact
points.body: Studies clearly show that communication failures are a leading cause of preventable adverse events during pediatric resuscitations.

points.heading: Effective Behaviors
points.body: Knowing your role, sharing information proactively, anticipating the next required interventions, and clear role delegation.

points.heading: The Big Picture
points.body: The Team Leader should avoid getting 'task fixated' and instead maintain a global view of the resuscitation effort.

points.heading: Debriefing
points.body: A hot debrief immediately after a code allows the team to discuss what went well, what could be improved, and provides emotional support.

points.heading: Simulation Training
points.body: Regular mock codes using high-fidelity simulation are the most evidence-based method for improving team dynamics and patient outcomes.

modules.title: Systematic Approach to the Seriously Ill or Injured Child
modules.subtitle: Assess, Evaluate, Intervene
learningObjectives: Perform a rapid visual assessment using the Pediatric Assessment Triangle (PAT).
Apply the Evaluate-Identify-Intervene sequence.
Conduct primary (ABCDE) and secondary (SAMPLE) assessments.
Recall normal pediatric vital signs.

points.heading: Purpose of the PAT
points.body: The PAT is an observational tool used from the doorway (no touching required) to form a rapid first impression of the child's physiological state within seconds.

points.heading: Appearance (TICLS)
points.body: Assess using TICLS: Tone, Interactiveness, Consolability, Look/gaze, Speech/cry.

points.heading: Work of Breathing
points.body: Look for nasal flaring, retractions (intercostal, subcostal, suprasternal), head bobbing, stridor, wheezing, or grunting.

points.heading: Circulation to Skin
points.body: Observe for pallor, mottling, or cyanosis.

quiz.stem: What does the 'C' in the TICLS mnemonic stand for?
quiz.rationale: C stands for Consolability, assessing if the child can be comforted by the caregiver.

quiz.stem: Which of the following is NOT a component of the Pediatric Assessment Triangle?
quiz.rationale: Blood pressure is not part of the PAT, which is purely a visual and auditory assessment requiring no equipment.

points.heading: Clinical Categorization
points.body: Combining normal/abnormal findings on the PAT allows providers to instantly categorize the patient into: Stable, Respiratory Distress, Respiratory Failure, Shock, or Primary CNS Dysfunction.

points.heading: Validation
points.body: The PAT has been extensively validated in both prehospital and emergency department settings as a highly sensitive tool for identifying critically ill children.

points.heading: Continuous Cycle
points.body: Evaluate the patient → Identify the problem → Intervene with appropriate treatment → Re-evaluate.

points.heading: Application
points.body: This sequence is applied continuously after the initial assessment. Never stop cycling through EII until the patient is stable and transferred to definitive care.

quiz.stem: What is the correct sequence of the continuous assessment cycle?
quiz.rationale: Evaluate the patient, Identify the specific physiological issue, then Intervene.

points.heading: Team Integration
points.body: The EII cycle maps perfectly onto team dynamics: The Team Leader Evaluates and Identifies, while team members execute the Interventions.

points.heading: Origins
points.body: Structured, algorithmic approaches like EII drastically reduce cognitive load during high-stress resuscitations.

points.heading: Airway & Breathing
points.body: Airway: Is it patent, maintainable, or unmaintainable? Breathing: Assess rate, effort (retractions, nasal flaring), chest expansion, SpO2, and listen for breath sounds.

points.heading: Circulation
points.body: Assess heart rate, blood pressure, pulse quality (central vs peripheral), capillary refill (normal <2 seconds), skin color/temp, and urine output.

points.heading: Disability
points.body: Assess using AVPU scale (Alert, Voice responsive, Pain responsive, Unresponsive), GCS, pupil size/reactivity, and ALWAYS check blood glucose.

points.heading: Exposure
points.body: Undress the patient to check temperature, rashes, petechiae, bruising, or signs of trauma.

quiz.stem: What does the AVPU scale measure during the 'Disability' phase?
quiz.rationale: AVPU (Alert, Voice, Pain, Unresponsive) is a rapid assessment of the child's level of consciousness.

quiz.stem: What is considered a normal capillary refill time in a pediatric patient?
quiz.rationale: Normal capillary refill time is less than 2 seconds.

points.heading: GCS Scoring
points.body: The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is used for a more detailed neurological assessment. Modifications exist for non-verbal infants and toddlers.

points.heading: Advanced Monitoring
points.body: While the ABCDE is primarily clinical, it integrates advanced monitoring like invasive arterial blood pressure, continuous waveform capnography, and continuous SpO2.

points.heading: SAMPLE History
points.body:
S = Signs and Symptoms
A = Allergies
M = Medications
P = Past medical history (include birth history for infants)
L = Last meal/intake
E = Events leading to current situation

points.heading: Timing
points.body: The secondary assessment (focused history and physical exam) is performed ONLY AFTER the primary assessment is complete and life-threatening issues are stabilized.

quiz.stem: What does the 'L' in the SAMPLE history stand for?
quiz.rationale: L stands for Last meal or liquid intake, important for aspiration risk.

quiz.stem: When should the secondary assessment be performed?
options: After the primary assessment is complete and the patient is stabilized
quiz.rationale: Secondary assessment is done after stabilizing ABCDEs.

points.heading: Focused vs Comprehensive
points.body: The secondary physical exam can be comprehensive (head-to-toe) or focused on the specific system implicated by the primary assessment and history.

points.heading: Documentation
points.body: Thorough documentation of the SAMPLE history is crucial for continuity of care when the patient is transferred to the PICU.

points.heading: Normal Ranges
points.body:
Neonate: HR 100-205, RR 30-60, SBP 67-84
Infant: HR 100-190, RR 30-53, SBP 72-104
Toddler: HR 98-140, RR 22-37, SBP 86-106
Preschool: HR 80-120, RR 20-28, SBP 89-112
School-age: HR 75-118, RR 18-25, SBP 97-120
Adolescent: HR 60-100, RR 12-20, SBP 110-131

points.heading: Defining Hypotension
points.body: Hypotension is defined as a systolic blood pressure < 5th percentile for age.

quiz.stem: What is the normal heart rate range for a toddler?
quiz.rationale: Toddler normal HR is 98-140/min.

quiz.stem: What is the quick calculation for the minimum normal systolic BP (5th percentile) for children 1-10 years old?
quiz.rationale: The formula is 70 + (2 × age in years).

points.heading: Hypotension Formula
points.body: For children 1 to 10 years old, use this quick formula to find the 5th percentile SBP: 70 + (2 × age in years).

points.heading: Weight Estimation
points.body: Broselow tapes or formulas like (Age x 2) + 8 = kg are used when a true weight cannot be obtained during an emergency.

points.heading: Percentile Tables
points.body: While formulas are useful, actual percentile-based BP tables indexed to height and sex are more accurate and should be referenced in the PICU/ED when possible.

modules.title: Recognizing Respiratory Problems
modules.subtitle: Distress vs. Failure
learningObjectives: Differentiate between upper and lower airway disease.
Distinguish respiratory distress from respiratory failure.

points.heading: Core Concept
points.body: Stridor indicates upper airway obstruction. Wheezing indicates lower airway obstruction.

points.heading: Core Concept
points.body: Failure involves inadequate oxygenation or ventilation despite compensatory mechanisms.

points.heading: Core Concept
points.body: Understand V/Q mismatch, shunt, and hypoventilation.

modules.title: Managing Respiratory Problems
modules.subtitle: Interventions for Oxygenation
learningObjectives: Select appropriate oxygen delivery devices.
Perform proper bag-mask ventilation.

points.heading: Oxygen
points.body: Titrate to appropriate targets.

points.heading: OPA and NPA
points.body: Use OPA for unconscious patients only.

points.heading: Technique
points.body: EC clamp technique is standard.

points.heading: ET Tubes
points.body: Secure the airway when BVM is insufficient.

points.heading: Asthma vs Croup
points.body: Specific pharmacology applies (albuterol vs racemic epi).

modules.title: Recognizing Shock
modules.subtitle: Identifying Inadequate Perfusion
learningObjectives: Recognize signs of compensated and hypotensive shock.

points.heading: Definition
points.body: Inadequate tissue delivery of oxygen and nutrients.

points.heading: Difference
points.body: Hypotension is a late and ominous sign in pediatrics.

points.heading: Types
points.body: Hypovolemic, Distributive, Cardiogenic, Obstructive.

points.heading: Stages
points.body: Mild, moderate, severe.

modules.title: Managing Shock
modules.subtitle: Restoring Perfusion
learningObjectives: Calculate fluid boluses.
Implement the septic shock algorithm.

points.heading: Primary Goal
points.body: Restore oxygen delivery.

points.heading: Bolus
points.body: 20 mL/kg isotonic crystalloid.

points.heading: Timing
points.body: Antibiotics within 1 hour.

points.heading: Epinephrine
points.body: Cold shock preference.

points.heading: Access
points.body: Early IO if IV fails.

modules.title: Recognizing Arrhythmias
modules.subtitle: ECG Interpretation Basics
learningObjectives: Identify normal sinus rhythm.
Differentiate SVT from Sinus Tachycardia.

points.heading: NSR
points.body: P wave before every QRS.

points.heading: Symptomatic
points.body: HR < 60 with poor perfusion.

points.heading: Differentiation
points.body: SVT usually >220 in infants, >180 in children.

points.heading: VT
points.body: Ventricular tachycardia is dangerous.

modules.title: Managing Arrhythmias
modules.subtitle: Algorithms and Interventions
learningObjectives: Apply the Bradycardia and Tachycardia algorithms.

points.heading: First step
points.body: Oxygen and ventilation.

points.heading: Vagal maneuvers
points.body: Try first if stable.

points.heading: Amiodarone
points.body: Pharmacologic choice.

points.heading: Cardioversion
points.body: Synchronized for unstable SVT/VT with a pulse.

modules.title: Cardiac Arrest
modules.subtitle: High-Quality CPR and Algorithms
learningObjectives: Perform shockable and nonshockable pathway algorithms.
Identify reversible causes (H's and T's).

points.heading: Origins
points.body: Mostly respiratory.

points.heading: VF/pVT
points.body: Defibrillate immediately.

points.heading: Asystole/PEA
points.body: Epinephrine early.

points.heading: Reversible Causes
points.body: Hypovolemia, Hypoxia, etc.

points.heading: Metrics
points.body: Minimize interruptions.

modules.title: Post-Cardiac Arrest Care
modules.subtitle: Optimizing Outcomes
learningObjectives: Set respiratory and cardiovascular goals post-arrest.

points.heading: Oxygen
points.body: Avoid hyperoxia.

points.heading: BP
points.body: Target >10th percentile.

points.heading: Temperature
points.body: Prevent hyperthermia.

points.heading: Survivorship
points.body: Long-term support.

modules.title: Integrated Assessment
modules.subtitle: Capstone Scenarios
learningObjectives: Integrate knowledge into practical scenarios.

points.heading: Application
points.body: Simulate respiratory failure.

points.heading: Application
points.body: Simulate shock progressing to arrest.

points.heading: Final Test
points.body: Must achieve 84% to pass.
